chapter_theme: Songs at Thiruvidaikkazhi (திருவிடைக்கழி), the shrine of the kura tree: the poet confesses useless learning, the body's hut, courtesans who take money and kick a man out, and the ocean of birth, and asks for the feet as a raft, the company of devotees and the gift of song; one song is a lovesick girl's plea for the kadamba garland, and the praise names Murugan teaching Siva and Brahma's prison.
structure_note: Learning and the body (792, 795, 796); patron-poets and the sea of birth (793); a list of boons (794); courtesans (797, 799); and an akam song (798) that takes its last lines from 797.

792.reading: The poet asks whether, not cherishing the hut of blood with fire and three gunas, and not learning sorrowful, anxious, useless arts without knowing their meaning, he must still be crushed in the corners of the eyes of cruel women who cajole and melt and join in union. The praise names Valli of the millet field, Murugan who told Siva with coral matted hair the one word to make him clear, the bright vel that split the golden-peaked hill, at Idaikkazhi where fish leap in the backwater.
792.nuance: சவலைக் கலை கற்று அதனிற் பொருள் சற்று அறியாதே: learning without knowing its meaning is joined to the body and to women as one wasted life. சிவனுக்கு ஒருசொல் பகர்வோனே is the guru-myth with Om not named. கடவேனோ, 'must I?', frames the whole first half as a question.

793.reading: The poet tells of the vanity of those who say 'I give generously to those who beg, even in dreams; which poet matches me in verse and music?', tie on turbans and rings and keep betel bags in lordly style, and of women who hide in their clothes faces, hair and brows likened to moon and cloud; to cross the ocean of birth that is mired in this hoof-print puddle, he asks for the raft of the golden feet. The praise shows the battle, the hills and seas dried, the gods returned to their city and Brahma imprisoned, Murugan at Idaikkazhi, and Valli in the millet field of pearls from tusks and bamboo, whom he took by the hand to the hunters' shame.
793.nuance: குளப்படியிற் சளப்படும் இப்பவக் கடல்: the ocean of birth is mocked as a hoof-print puddle, and yet the feet are needed as a raft (கழற் புணை) to cross it. The boasting in the first lines may be the poet's own or that of patrons; the reading leaves it open.

794.reading: The poet asks for a list of gifts: the meaning of the three Tamils, the fruit of true austerity, many kinds of life, the ancient state of release, the life of the wish-tree, a faultless mind, kingship and a wondrous great life, and with the senses gone, the strength of praise. The praise names Murugan of the Saravana pool, who embraced the hunter girl in the lone forest and split the peaked hill, at Idaikkazhi of the kura groves.
794.nuance: The plea is all asking, with no confession; worldly gifts (அரசு, கற்பகத்தரு வாழ்வு) sit beside release (முத்தியிற் பதம்) and end in புகழ் பலம், the power of praise, the poet's own gift. புலன் அகற்றிட: the senses removed.

795.reading: The poet describes the body of earth, water, fire, wind and space, the false embryo, the states, the three gunas, diseases, marrow, semen, blood, bone and fat, a hungry hut, and confesses that, bearing it in a birth low in virtue without an aware mind, he wanders; he asks for the pair of feet and a place among Murugan's own people. The praise names the cock banner, Valli's arms, Murugan the son of the true father, poet of the three Tamils, at Idaikkazhi which grants release.
795.nuance: The catalogue mixes the elements, the states of consciousness (அவத்தை) and the three gunas with the body's fluids, a doctrinal and a physical body in one list. உனது தமர் ஒக்க வைத்து: be set among your people. The praise lines on the battle and the elephant (தடவிகட மத்தகத் தடவரை) are hard to divide.

796.reading: The poet confesses that, carrying the blamed hut of the body, he fell into the pit of illusion women offer and gropes for the way out, that the world's fools babble of old things, and that he sought many useless arts without grasping the one meaning; before he dies he asks to seek the lotus feet, melt with nectar welling in his heart and sing Murugan's holy praise. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, the sea churning, Meru shaking and the gods crying victory, the kadamba-wearing Saravana on the peacock, lord of Arunai, Tiruttani, Nagamalai, Palani, Kodai and Idaikkazhi.
796.nuance: ஒருபயனைத் தெளியாது: learning without the one aim is the fault, as in 792. உனது திருப்புகழ் ஓத (written திருப்புழோத) asks for the poet's book by name. The list of shrines at the close makes Idaikkazhi one of Murugan's many seats.

797.reading: The poet describes women who laugh and say 'come' when a wealthy man arrives, take his finger to the bed, play thigh to thigh, babble and talk sweetly until the agreed money reaches their place, and lull him to sleep on their breasts; when his wealth ends they twist round, kick and abuse him, and he asks that the work of these traitors end and he be driven to worship the two flower feet. The praise shows the vel that killed the asuras from the peacock's back, Murugan the son of Siva, who plucked Brahma's head with a nail, smiled at the triple city and gives grace in his devotees' thought, embracing the hunter girl on a fragrant bed, under the kura tree praised by sages, Indra and Brahma.
797.nuance: பொருள் தீரின் முறுக்கியே உதை கொடு வசை உரைதரு: the expulsion when the money runs out is shown as a physical kick, the courtesan story told at its harshest. திருக்குராவடி நிழல், the shade of the holy kura tree, is the sthala tree of Idaikkazhi, named again in 798.

798.reading: In another's voice, the singer asks that the fragrant flower bed not burn the girl, that the mother who raised her and her kin not speak blame, and that the neighbours not slander her, and asks Murugan to send his kadamba garland now. The praise names the husband of the creeper-waisted girl, the hero on the emerald peacock, who dwells in the shade of the holy kura tree, with the beautiful vel in hand.
798.nuance: The three dangers are the bed (கொதியாதே), the family's blame (வசை) and the neighbours' gossip (அயலவர் பழி), so the garland is asked to stop talk as well as longing. The eight lines take their praise words from 797 (மருக்குலாவிய மலரணை, திருக்குராவடி நிழல், திருக்கை வேல் வடிவழகிய).

799.reading: The poet heaps names on the women: breast-shakers, deceivers, dull ones, thieves, coaxers, mockers, fakers who weep, women who loosen their clothes and take young men's wealth, give half a betel roll in union and then abuse; he asks for grace so that the worry of losing himself in their bewitching eyes may end. The praise shows the hill turned to dust and the Jains impaled by the peacock hero, Murugan who told Siva, Vishnu and Brahma each a meaning, nephew of Rama who broke the bow at Mithila and won Sita, at Idaikkazhi of jackfruit, areca and plantain.
799.nuance: இளைஞர்கள் பொருள் பறித்த and ஒருபாதி வெற்றிலைச் சுருள் (half a betel roll) mark these as courtesans who take much and give little. அவரவர்க்கு ஒரு பொருள் புகல் பெரியோனே widens the guru-myth to all three gods. சமணர்கள் குலம் அணி கழுப்பெற gives the impaling of the Jains to the peacock hero.

links.note: The Naladiyar's harlots' love ends when the hand is empty, as the lamp's light ends with the oil; 797 shows the same end acted out, the man twisted round, kicked and abused once his wealth is gone.

Both are pleas in another's voice for a lovesick girl, worn by the flower bed and by women's blame, asking Murugan for his garland; 798 adds the neighbours' slander and asks for the kadamba garland by name.

The fragrant flower bed (மருக்குலாவிய மலரணை) is in 797 the bed where Murugan embraces Valli and in 798 the bed that burns the girl who longs for him; the two songs share the kura tree and the vel in their closing lines.

792 counts among its wasted years having learned useless arts without grasping a little of their meaning (சவலைக் கலை கற்று அதனிற் பொருள் சற்று அறியாதே). Naladiyar 135 gives the reason this is ruinous: learning has no shore and the learner's days are few (கல்வி கரையில கற்பவர் நாள்சில), so one must choose like the bird that drinks the milk and leaves the water. The quatrain supplies the rule whose breach 792 confesses.

793 opens on the voice of a man who boasts 'which poet matches me in verse and music' (எனக்கு இயலுக்கு இசைக்கு எதிர் எப்புலவோர்) and takes on turban, rings and betel bag in lordly style, and sets this vanity among the things that mire him in the puddle of birth. 935 lists the same court poet's honours, crown, whisks, the title கவிராஜ, but uses them as the argument for refusing to praise unworthy men (பஞ்ச பாதகரைப் புகழ் செயலாமோ). The poet's pride is a snare in one song and a ground for refusal in the other.

794 asks Murugan for a list of gifts that begins with the meaning of the three Tamils (பகரு முத்தமிழ்ப் பொருள்) and ends with the strength of praise (புகழ் பலத்தினைத் தரவேணும்). Tirumular says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ்செய்யு மாறே). Tirumular states as done what Arunagiri still asks for: Tamil praise as the purpose for which the poet is made.

795 catalogues the body as the five elements (படி புனல் நெருப்பு அடல் பவனம் வெளி), the states (அவத்தை), the three gunas, diseases and the fluids, to confess the life he bears in it. Tirumanthiram 2146 gives the doctrinal count behind such a list: elements, senses, malas, gunas and the adharas make up the ninety-six instruments of the first state (ஆதி அவத்தைக் கருவி தொண்ணூற்றாறே). The pairing shows the poet's list drawing on the Siddhanta tally of tattvas, mixed with the body's fluids.

796 confesses seeking many useless arts without grasping the one fruit (பலசவலைக் கலைதேடி ஒருபயனைத் தெளியாது) and asks, before death, to seek the lotus feet. Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not worship the good feet (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல் ... நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்). Both name the feet as the one fruit (பயன்) that learning exists for; the song is the Kural's question answered as a confession.

797 shows the courtesan coaxing with sweet words until the money reaches her, then, when the wealth ends, twisting round to kick and abuse (பொருள்தீரின் முறுக்கியே உதை கொடு வசை உரைதரு). Naladiyar 377 has her lick like a wild cow, take the wealth from his hands, then balk like a stubborn ox (ஆமாபோல் நக்கி ... சேமாபோல் குப்புறூஉம்). Both turn on the same reversal, fondness while the wealth is in hand and a physical turning away after it.

798, in a girl's voice, asks Murugan to send his kadamba garland so that the mother who raised her will not speak blame (வளர்த்த தாய் தமர் வசையது மொழியாதே) and the neighbours will not slander her (அயலவர் பழியாதே). Kural 1147 names the same two voices as what feeds the lovesickness: the town's gossip its manure and the mother's word its water (ஊரவர் கெளவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல் நீராக). The song asks the god to stop exactly what in the Kural makes the sickness grow.

799 heaps names on the courtesans, among them women with weeping hearts (அழு மனத்திகள்) and those who take young men's wealth (இளைஞர்கள் பொருள் பறித்த). Naladiyar 372 tells one such scene: the woman who vowed to leap from the peak with him, finding he had no gold, showed a pain in her feet and wept (காற்கால்நோய் காட்டிக் கலுழ்ந்து). The quatrain gives the story behind the poet's one-word epithet for tears used as a feint.

source_issues: Song 796: unflagged garbles பிதற் றிடுலொக ...... மு முடர் (line 4, probably பிதற்றிடும் உலக மூடர், 'the babbling fools of the world') and திருப் புழோத (line 8, probably திருப்புகழ் ஓத).
Song 795: the praise lines தடவிகட மத்தகத் தடவரைய ரத்தரத் தடலனுச (lines 13 to 14) are hard to divide and may be garbled.
